meta.subject: english
meta.description: Phonics facts: vowel sounds, consonant blends, digraphs, syllable types, silent letters, spelling, r-controlled vowels, diphthongs, word families, sight words, morphology

facts.statement: The five vowels in English are A, E, I, O, U; the letter Y sometimes acts as a vowel
Short vowels make the sounds in: cat (a), bed (e), sit (i), hot (o), cup (u)
Long vowels say their own name: cake (a), feet (e), kite (i), rope (o), cube (u)
The silent e at the end of a word often makes the preceding vowel long: hat/hate, bit/bite, hop/hope
Vowel teams are two vowels together that make one sound: 'ea' in read, 'oa' in boat, 'ai' in rain
The schwa is the most common vowel sound in English, a lazy 'uh' sound heard in unstressed syllables: 'a' in about, 'e' in taken
A diphthong is a vowel sound that glides from one sound to another: 'oi' in coin, 'ou' in house
The vowel team 'oo' can make two different sounds: a long sound as in 'moon' and a short sound as in 'book'
When Y appears at the end of a one-syllable word, it usually makes the long 'i' sound: fly, try, sky, dry
When Y appears at the end of a multi-syllable word, it usually makes the long 'e' sound: happy, funny, baby, candy

common_errors.wrong: every word with a silent e has a long vowel
common_errors.correct: Some words with silent e do not follow the pattern: have, give, love, some, come.

common_errors.wrong: y is always a consonant
common_errors.correct: Y acts as a vowel in words like 'gym,' 'fly,' 'happy,' and 'myth.' It is a consonant at the beginning of words like 'yes' and 'yellow.'

common_errors.wrong: the rule 'when two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking' always works
common_errors.correct: This rule has many exceptions: 'bread,' 'said,' 'chief.' It works about 45% of the time.

common_errors.wrong: all vowel teams make a long vowel sound
common_errors.correct: Some vowel teams make other sounds: 'oo' in 'book' is not a long vowel, 'ow' in 'cow' is a diphthong, and 'ea' in 'bread' is short e.

facts.statement: A consonant blend is two or three consonants together where each sound can be heard: bl, cr, str, spl
A consonant digraph is two consonants together that make one new sound: ch, sh, th, wh, ph, ck, ng
'Ch' makes the sound in 'chair,' 'sh' makes the sound in 'ship,' 'th' makes the sound in 'think' or 'the'
'Ph' makes the 'f' sound as in 'phone' and 'photo'
The 'th' digraph has two sounds: voiced (as in 'the,' 'this,' 'that') and unvoiced (as in 'think,' 'thin,' 'three')
Common beginning blends include: bl, br, cl, cr, dr, fl, fr, gl, gr, pl, pr, sc, sk, sl, sm, sn, sp, st, sw, tr
Common ending blends include: -nd (hand), -nk (think), -nt (went), -mp (jump), -ft (left), -lt (belt), -lk (milk)
Three-letter blends appear at the beginning of words: str (street), spl (splash), spr (spring), scr (scratch), squ (square)
The digraph 'ck' appears at the end of a short word after a short vowel: back, neck, kick, lock, duck
The digraph 'ng' makes a nasal sound at the end of words: ring, song, lung, hang, king

common_errors.wrong: blends and digraphs are the same thing
common_errors.correct: In a blend, you hear each consonant sound (bl = b + l). In a digraph, two letters make one new sound (sh is one sound, not s + h).

common_errors.wrong: 'qu' is a digraph
common_errors.correct: 'Qu' is technically a consonant team, not a digraph. The 'u' typically represents the /w/ sound: queen = kw-een.

common_errors.wrong: the letter 'c' always makes the same sound
common_errors.correct: 'C' makes a hard sound (like 'k') before a, o, u (cat, cot, cup) and a soft sound (like 's') before e, i, y (cent, city, cycle).

common_errors.wrong: the letter 'g' always makes the same sound
common_errors.correct: 'G' makes a hard sound before a, o, u (game, go, gum) and often a soft sound (like 'j') before e, i, y (gem, giant, gym), though there are exceptions like 'get' and 'give.'

facts.statement: Every syllable must contain at least one vowel sound
A closed syllable ends in a consonant and the vowel is usually short: cat, nap, pen, sit
An open syllable ends in a vowel and the vowel is usually long: me, go, hi, she, no
An r-controlled syllable has a vowel followed by 'r,' changing the vowel sound: car, bird, her, for, fur
A consonant-le syllable appears at the end of a word: ta-ble, sim-ple, puz-zle, can-dle
To count syllables, count the number of vowel sounds (not vowel letters) in a word
There are six syllable types in English: closed, open, vowel-consonant-e, vowel team, r-controlled, and consonant-le
In a VCCV pattern (vowel-consonant-consonant-vowel), usually divide between the two consonants: nap-kin, rab-bit, pic-nic
In a VCV pattern (vowel-consonant-vowel), first try dividing before the consonant for an open syllable: mo-tor, pa-per, pi-lot
A vowel-consonant-e syllable has a long vowel followed by a consonant and a silent e: make, theme, pine, home, cute

common_errors.wrong: the number of vowel letters equals the number of syllables
common_errors.correct: Count vowel sounds, not letters. 'Cake' has two vowel letters but one syllable. 'Area' has three vowel letters and three syllables.

common_errors.wrong: all two-letter words are one syllable
common_errors.correct: Most two-letter words are one syllable, but 'io' words in some languages can be two.

common_errors.wrong: silent letters count as separate syllables
common_errors.correct: Silent letters do not produce sounds and do not create syllables. The 'e' in 'cake' is silent.

common_errors.wrong: consonant-le syllables have a vowel sound from the 'e'
common_errors.correct: In consonant-le syllables (like 'ta-ble'), the 'e' is silent. The syllable's vowel sound comes from the 'schwa' or is very reduced.

facts.statement: Common silent letters include: k in 'knee,' w in 'write,' b in 'comb,' h in 'honest,' g in 'gnaw'
The 'i before e except after c' rule applies when the sound is 'ee': receive, believe, ceiling, but has many exceptions like weird, seize, neither
When adding a suffix beginning with a vowel to a word ending in silent e, usually drop the e: make/making, hope/hoping
When a one-syllable word ends in a single consonant after a single short vowel, double the consonant before adding a vowel suffix: run/running, sit/sitting
To make most nouns plural, add -s; for words ending in s, sh, ch, x, z, add -es; for words ending in consonant+y, change y to i and add -es
Some words have irregular plurals that do not follow standard rules: child/children, mouse/mice, tooth/teeth, person/people, foot/feet
The '-igh' pattern makes the long 'i' sound: night, light, right, fight, sight, high
The '-ough' pattern can make many different sounds: though (long o), through (oo), thought (aw), rough (uf), cough (off)
Words ending in 'f' or 'fe' often change to 'v' before adding '-es' for the plural: knife/knives, leaf/leaves, wolf/wolves
When adding a suffix to a word ending in consonant+y, change the y to i: happy/happiness, carry/carried, beauty/beautiful

common_errors.wrong: 'i before e except after c' is always correct
common_errors.correct: This rule has many common exceptions: weird, seize, neither, leisure, protein, caffeine, forfeit.

common_errors.wrong: you always add -s to make a plural
common_errors.correct: Words ending in s, sh, ch, x, or z need -es. Words ending in consonant+y change y to i before -es. Some words have irregular plurals.

common_errors.wrong: hopping and hoping have the same number of p's
common_errors.correct: Hopping (jumping) has two p's; hoping (wishing) has one p. Doubling the consonant keeps the vowel short.

common_errors.wrong: silent letters serve no purpose and are random
common_errors.correct: Silent letters often reflect a word's history and origin. 'Knight' once had the 'k' and 'gh' pronounced in Old English.

facts.statement: R-controlled vowels (also called 'bossy r') occur when a vowel is followed by the letter 'r,' which changes the vowel sound
The 'ar' combination makes the sound heard in car, star, farm, park, and dark
The combinations 'er,' 'ir,' and 'ur' all make the same sound as heard in her, bird, and fur
The 'or' combination makes the sound heard in for, corn, short, sport, and born
The combination 'ore' makes the long 'or' sound: more, store, before, shore, score
The combination 'air' and 'are' make the same sound: chair/care, fair/fare, pair/pare
The combination 'ear' can make different sounds: hear (long e + r), bear (air sound), earn (er sound)
R-controlled vowels are neither short nor long vowels; they are a distinct category of vowel sounds
The 'war' and 'wor' combinations often make the same sound as 'or': warm, war, word, work, world, worm
In the word 'dollar,' the 'ar' at the end sounds like the 'er' sound, not the typical 'ar' sound as in 'car'

common_errors.wrong: er, ir, and ur make different sounds
common_errors.correct: The combinations 'er' (her), 'ir' (bird), and 'ur' (fur) all produce the same vowel sound in standard American English.

common_errors.wrong: r-controlled vowels are just short vowels with an r after them
common_errors.correct: The 'r' changes the vowel sound entirely. The 'a' in 'car' sounds nothing like the short 'a' in 'cat.' R-controlled vowels are their own category.

common_errors.wrong: 'ear' always makes the same sound
common_errors.correct: 'Ear' can sound different in different words: hear (eer), bear (air), earn (er). Context determines the pronunciation.

facts.statement: A diphthong is a complex vowel sound that glides from one vowel position to another within the same syllable
The diphthong 'oi' and 'oy' make the same sound: coin, oil, boil, boy, toy, joy
The diphthong 'ou' and 'ow' make the same sound in words like: out, house, mouse, cow, how, now
'Oi' typically appears in the middle of a word (coin, point) while 'oy' typically appears at the end (boy, enjoy)
'Ou' typically appears in the middle of a word (house, loud) while 'ow' can appear at the end (cow, now) or in the middle (down, town)
The letters 'ow' can make two different sounds: the diphthong in 'cow' and the long 'o' sound in 'snow'
Diphthongs are different from vowel teams because they produce a gliding sound rather than a single pure vowel sound
The word 'diphthong' comes from Greek, meaning 'two sounds' or 'two voices'
The diphthong 'ew' as in 'few' and 'new' glides from one vowel position to the 'oo' sound
English has four main diphthong sounds: /oi/ as in boy, /ou/ as in cow, /ai/ as in fly, and /au/ as in house

common_errors.wrong: diphthongs and vowel teams are the same thing
common_errors.correct: Vowel teams make one pure sound (like 'ai' in rain = long a). Diphthongs glide between two sounds (like 'oi' in coin starts at one vowel and slides to another).

common_errors.wrong: 'ow' always makes the same sound
common_errors.correct: 'Ow' makes the diphthong sound in 'cow' and 'how' but the long 'o' sound in 'snow' and 'show.' You must use context to determine which.

common_errors.wrong: diphthongs are two separate vowel sounds in two syllables
common_errors.correct: A diphthong is one syllable where the vowel sound glides smoothly from one position to another, not two separate syllables.

facts.statement: A word family is a group of words that share the same ending pattern (rime): cat, hat, bat, sat, mat all belong to the '-at' family
The onset is the consonant(s) before the vowel in a syllable; the rime is the vowel and everything after it: in 'cat,' 'c' is the onset and 'at' is the rime
Learning word families helps children decode new words by recognizing patterns: knowing '-ake' helps read cake, make, lake, take, bake
Common short vowel word families include: -at, -an, -ap, -ad, -ag, -et, -en, -ig, -in, -it, -op, -ot, -ug, -un, -ut
Common long vowel word families include: -ake, -ame, -ate, -ine, -ite, -ide, -oke, -one, -ube, -ute
Words in the same word family rhyme because they share the same vowel sound and ending consonants
There are approximately 37 common word families (rimes) in English that can be used to generate about 500 common words
Changing the onset of a word family pattern creates a new word: replacing 'c' in 'cat' with 'b' makes 'bat'

common_errors.wrong: word families and rhyming words are completely different concepts
common_errors.correct: Word families and rhyming words overlap: words in the same family (cat, hat, bat) do rhyme. However, some rhyming words have different spelling patterns (great, late).

common_errors.wrong: all words that end with the same letters are in the same word family
common_errors.correct: Words must share the same ending SOUND pattern. 'Low' and 'cow' end with 'ow' but sound different, so they are in different word families.

common_errors.wrong: word families only apply to three-letter words
common_errors.correct: Word families work with longer words too: the '-ake' family includes cake, brake, snowflake, and mistake.

facts.statement: Sight words are common words that children learn to recognize instantly without sounding them out, such as 'the,' 'and,' 'is,' 'was'
Many sight words are irregularly spelled and cannot be decoded using standard phonics rules: 'said,' 'was,' 'the,' 'of,' 'come'
The Dolch word list contains 220 high-frequency words organized by grade level from pre-primer through third grade
The Fry word list contains the 1,000 most common English words; the first 100 Fry words make up about 50% of all written text
Some sight words follow phonics rules but appear so frequently that instant recognition speeds up reading: 'and,' 'can,' 'not,' 'but'
The word 'the' is the most common word in the English language, appearing in almost every sentence
Sight words are also called high-frequency words because they appear very often in books and everyday reading
Children typically learn sight words through repeated exposure, flashcards, reading practice, and writing the words
Common pre-primer sight words include: a, and, the, I, is, it, in, my, to, we, can, see, go, like, you
By the end of first grade, most students are expected to recognize approximately 100 high-frequency sight words automatically

common_errors.wrong: sight words cannot be sounded out at all
common_errors.correct: Some sight words ARE decodable ('and,' 'not,' 'can') but are taught as sight words for fluency. Others ARE truly irregular ('said,' 'the,' 'was').

common_errors.wrong: sight words are only for beginning readers
common_errors.correct: While sight word instruction focuses on early grades, readers of all levels benefit from automatic recognition of high-frequency words for reading fluency.

common_errors.wrong: memorizing sight words means phonics is not important
common_errors.correct: Phonics and sight words work together. Phonics teaches children to decode most words, while sight words cover the irregular and very common words that don't follow rules.

facts.statement: A morpheme is the smallest unit of meaning in a word; 'cats' has two morphemes: 'cat' (the animal) + 's' (plural)
A base word (or root word) is a word that can stand alone and has meaning by itself: 'play' is the base in 'replay' and 'playing'
An inflectional suffix changes the form of a word without changing its part of speech: -s (cats), -ed (walked), -ing (running), -er (taller), -est (tallest)
A derivational affix changes the meaning or part of speech of a word: 'happy' (adjective) + '-ness' = 'happiness' (noun)
A compound word is made by joining two smaller words together: sunshine (sun + shine), bedroom (bed + room), football (foot + ball)
The prefix 'un-' means 'not' or 'opposite': unhappy, unkind, unlock, undo, unfair
The prefix 're-' means 'again': rewrite, redo, replay, reread, rebuild
The suffix '-er' can mean 'one who does' (teacher, runner) or 'more' in comparisons (taller, faster)
Adding the suffix '-ed' to a verb puts it in the past tense: walk/walked, jump/jumped, play/played
The suffix '-ed' can make three different sounds: /t/ as in 'walked,' /d/ as in 'played,' and /id/ as in 'wanted'

common_errors.wrong: a prefix changes the spelling of the base word
common_errors.correct: Adding a prefix does not change the base word's spelling: un + happy = unhappy, mis + spell = misspell (the double 's' is correct, not a change).

common_errors.wrong: every long word has a prefix or suffix
common_errors.correct: Some long words are single morphemes from other languages (chocolate, banana, dinosaur) and do not contain English prefixes or suffixes.

common_errors.wrong: compound words always have no space between them
common_errors.correct: Compound words can be closed (sunflower), hyphenated (well-known), or open (ice cream). All three forms are compound words.

common_errors.wrong: the suffix '-ed' always adds a syllable to a word
common_errors.correct: The '-ed' ending only adds a syllable when the base word ends in 't' or 'd': wanted, painted. In 'walked' and 'played,' '-ed' does not add a syllable.
